name: ML
year_note: Design began in 1973 as the metalanguage of the Edinburgh LCF theorem prover; LCF/ML was finalised in the book 'Edinburgh LCF' (1979). Standard ML was proposed in 1983, formally defined in 1990 and revised in 1997 (SML '97).
tagline: The metalanguage of a theorem prover that gave programming Hindley–Milner type inference, polymorphism and safe abstract types.
summary: ML is a statically typed functional language created by Robin Milner's group at Edinburgh as the 'meta language' for scripting proofs in the LCF theorem prover. It combined first-class functions with a polymorphic type system whose types are inferred automatically, together with exceptions and abstract types that guaranteed theorems could only be produced by valid inference rules. Its descendants — Standard ML, Caml/OCaml and F# — and its type system shaped nearly every typed functional language that followed.
history:
Milner started the Edinburgh LCF project around 1973 to build a more extensible successor to Stanford LCF, working first with Lockwood Morris and Malcolm Newey and, from 1975, with Michael Gordon and Christopher Wadsworth. ML was designed as its metalanguage: proof tactics were ML functions, 'tacticals' were higher-order functions, failing tactics raised exceptions, and theorems were an abstract type whose only constructors were the inference rules, so static typing made proofs unforgeable. LCF/ML was implemented by translation into Stanford Lisp and documented in the book 'Edinburgh LCF' (1979); Milner's 1978 paper 'A Theory of Type Polymorphism in Programming' gave its type inference algorithm.

Dialects soon diverged — Luca Cardelli's VAX ML, and Gérard Huet's version at INRIA, which led to Caml — while Rod Burstall's related language HOPE introduced algebraic datatypes with pattern matching. In 1983 Milner proposed 'Standard ML', uniting LCF/ML with HOPE's datatypes and clausal function definitions, and David MacQueen designed its module system of signatures, structures and functors. 'The Definition of Standard ML' (Milner, Tofte and Harper, 1990; revised 1997) made it one of the few practical languages with a complete formal semantics. Standard ML lives on in SML/NJ, MLton and Poly/ML, and the family continues through OCaml and F#.
innovations: Hindley–Milner type inference: full static typing with no annotations (Milner 1978; Damas and Milner 1982)
Parametric polymorphism with inferred type variables ('a list, 'a -> 'a)
Abstract types as a security mechanism: LCF's theorem type could be built only by inference rules
Typed exception handling, designed so failing proof tactics could be caught and retried
In Standard ML: algebraic datatypes with exhaustively checked pattern matching
In Standard ML: a module system of signatures, structures and functors, and a complete formal definition (1990)

typing.notes: Hindley–Milner inference with let-polymorphism; SML '97 adds the value restriction for mutable references. Datatypes are generative (nominal); records and tuples are structural.

latest_version: Standard ML '97 (The Definition of Standard ML, Revised)

influenced_by.note: Stanford LCF was written in Lisp and LCF/ML was implemented by translation into Stanford Lisp; type inference kept much of the fluency of Lisp while adding static types and proper closures.

influenced_by_external.name: ISWIM
influenced_by_external.note: Landin's applicative language: ML's call-by-value core and let/where-style declarations.

influenced_by_external.name: POP-2
influenced_by_external.note: Popplestone and Burstall's Edinburgh AI language: records, partial application and an escape mechanism.

influenced_by_external.name: GEDANKEN
influenced_by_external.note: Reynolds's language with references as first-class values.

influenced_by_external.name: HOPE
influenced_by_external.note: Burstall's Edinburgh language; source of Standard ML's datatypes, pattern matching and clausal definitions.

generics.note: Parametric polymorphism ('a list); Standard ML functors add module-level genericity.

immutability.note: Bindings and data are immutable; mutation needs explicit ref cells (LCF/ML used letref variables).

option-types.note: The 'a option datatype (NONE | SOME v) in the Basis Library; there are no null references. LCF/ML had binary sum types (ty1 + ty2).

first-class-functions.note: Tactics as functions and tacticals as higher-order functions were the original motivation.

closures.note: Lexically scoped closures from the start, unlike the dynamically scoped Lisps of the time.

exceptions.note: LCF/ML had failwith and ? failure trapping; Standard ML has typed exceptions with raise/handle.

abstract-data-types.note: LCF/ML's abstype (used for LCF's theorem type); SML '97 adds opaque signature ascription (:>).

pattern-matching.note: Clausal function definitions over datatype constructors, adopted from HOPE (via NPL); LCF/ML had no datatypes to match on.

algebraic-data-types.note: datatype declarations adopted from HOPE, with exhaustiveness checking.

modules.note: MacQueen's signatures, structures and functors, proposed in 1984 and fixed in the 1990 Definition.

interfaces.note: Signatures specify module interfaces; one structure can match many signatures.

structural-typing.note: Record and tuple types, and signature matching, are structural; datatypes are not.

block-scope.note: let … in … end and local … in … end.

structured-control.note: if and case expressions and while loops, though recursion is idiomatic.

tail-calls.note: Not required by the Definition, but guaranteed in practice by the major implementations.

continuations.note: callcc in SML/NJ (SMLofNJ.Cont) and MLton (MLton.Cont); not part of the Definition.

csp-channels.note: Concurrent ML (Reppy, 1991): synchronous channels and first-class events on SML/NJ and MLton.

milestones.event: Milner starts the Edinburgh LCF project; ML is designed as its metalanguage
Milner's 'A Theory of Type Polymorphism in Programming' presents algorithm W
Damas and Milner prove principal types for ML's type system (POPL)
Milner proposes Standard ML, adding HOPE-style datatypes and pattern matching
MacQueen's module system and Milner's core-language proposal presented at LFP

Revised Definition (SML '97): value restriction, opaque signatures, new Basis Library

trivia: ML stands for 'Meta Language': the language in which LCF users wrote proof procedures about the object logic.
A Springer-Verlag form-filling bug credited the 1979 book 'Edinburgh LCF' to 'Arthur J. Milner'.
HOPE, whose datatypes Standard ML adopted, is not an acronym: it is named after Hope Park Square in Edinburgh, where it was born.

hello.notes: Run as a script with Poly/ML. In the original LCF/ML, top-level phrases ended with ';;' and strings were 'tokens'.

factorial.code:
fun factorial 0 = 1
  | factorial n = n * factorial (n - 1)

val () = print (Int.toString (factorial 10) ^ "\n")
factorial.notes: Clausal definitions by pattern matching arrived with Standard ML (from HOPE); LCF/ML would have written roughly letrec fact n = if n = 0 then 1 else n * fact (n - 1);;

fizzbuzz.code:
fun fizzbuzz n =
  case (n mod 3, n mod 5) of
      (0, 0) => "FizzBuzz"
    | (0, _) => "Fizz"
    | (_, 0) => "Buzz"
    | _      => Int.toString n

val () =
  List.app (fn n => print (fizzbuzz n ^ "\n"))
           (List.tabulate (15, fn i => i + 1))
fizzbuzz.expected_output:
1
2
Fizz
4
Buzz
Fizz
7
8
Fizz
Buzz
11
Fizz
13
14
FizzBuzz
fizzbuzz.notes: case over a tuple of remainders. LCF/ML had no case expression; it used nested if-then-else (and could iterate with its combined if … loop construct).

higher-order.code:
val nums = List.tabulate (10, fn i => i + 1)

val squares =
  List.map (fn x => x * x) (List.filter (fn x => x mod 2 = 0) nums)

val () = print (String.concatWith " " (List.map Int.toString squares) ^ "\n")
higher-order.notes: List.tabulate, List.map, List.filter and String.concatWith come from the SML '97 Basis Library.

shapes.code:
(* An algebraic data type: a shape is one of two tagged variants. *)
datatype shape =
    Rectangle of {width : int, height : int}
  | Triangle of {base : int, height : int}

(* Clausal definitions dispatch on the constructor; the compiler
   checks the match is exhaustive. *)
fun area (Rectangle {width, height}) = width * height
  | area (Triangle {base, height})   = base * height div 2

fun name (Rectangle _) = "Rectangle"
  | name (Triangle _)  = "Triangle"

val () =
  List.app (fn s => print (name s ^ ": " ^ Int.toString (area s) ^ "\n"))
           [Rectangle {width = 3, height = 4}, Triangle {base = 10, height = 3}]
shapes.notes: datatype plus pattern matching came from HOPE into Standard ML, and the record syntax from Cardelli's VAX ML; LCF/ML offered only abstract types and binary sums.

signature.title: Types without annotations
signature.code:
(* Not one type annotation: Hindley-Milner inference finds the most
   general type of each definition (shown in the comments). *)

(* compose : ('a -> 'b) * ('c -> 'a) -> 'c -> 'b *)
fun compose (f, g) x = f (g x)

(* foldr : ('a * 'b -> 'b) -> 'b -> 'a list -> 'b *)
fun foldr f z []        = z
  | foldr f z (x :: xs) = f (x, foldr f z xs)

(* length : 'a list -> int -- works on a list of anything *)
fun length xs = foldr (fn (_, n) => n + 1) 0 xs

(* sum : int list -> int  *)
fun sum xs = foldr (op +) 0 xs

(* The same polymorphic code, used at several types. *)
val () = print (Int.toString (length ["a", "b", "c"]) ^ "\n")
val () = print (Int.toString (length [true, false]) ^ "\n")
val () = print (compose (Int.toString, sum) [1, 2, 3, 4] ^ "\n")
val () = print (foldr (op ^) "" ["M", "L"] ^ "\n")
signature.notes: The types in the comments are exactly what Poly/ML's REPL reports for these definitions. foldr and length deliberately shadow the Basis versions to show inference on user code.
